metadata.document: Submission on the Proposed Regulatory Standards Bill

cleaned_body_text: Submission details: Environmental Defence Society Incorporated, PO Box 91736, Victoria Street West, Auckland 1042. Attn: Shay Schlaepfer / John Commissaris. Introduction: The Environmental Defence Society Incorporated (EDS) is an environmental non-government organisation focused on legal advocacy and policy research. It is dedicated to improving environmental outcomes for all New Zealanders. EDS’s submission on the Proposed Regulatory Standards Bill (Proposed Bill) is formed through that lens. Summary of submission: EDS considers regulation to be an important tool to protect the natural environment while enabling communities to thrive. To be effective, regulations and regulatory processes should be strategic, transparent, proportionate, based on evidence, and maintained and updated as needed. Improving regulatory efficacy is supported. The outline of the Proposed Bill does not address key factors that can undermine regulatory efficacy in Aotearoa New Zealand. Rather, like its predecessors, the Proposed Bill entrenches a set of selective and subjective ‘principles of responsible regulation’ (Principles) that have the potential to make things significantly worse. EDS opposes the Proposed Bill for three key reasons: the Principles are flawed, driven by contentious ideology, leave significant gaps, and fail to acknowledge fundamental and internationally recognised tenets of good regulatory decision-making; the powers vested in the Minister for Regulation are excessive and inappropriate; and the Proposed Bill cuts across existing and soon-to-be-implemented frameworks, including Part 4 of the Legislation Act 2019, adding significant costs without a detailed assessment of any associated benefits. Overall, the Proposed Bill represents a powerful constitutional shift that undermines collective interests, environmental protection and Te Tiriti o Waitangi / Treaty of Waitangi. Proposed Bill: The Proposed Bill seeks to address concerns about New Zealand’s current regulatory oversight arrangements and to improve the quality of regulation. Genesis: The idea of a Regulatory Standards Bill was first proposed in 2006 when the Regulatory Responsibility Bill was introduced as a private member’s Bill. It did not pass its first reading. In 2009, the Government established the Regulatory Responsibility Taskforce to consider what should be in a Regulatory Standards Bill. The Taskforceʼs Bill formed the basis of the Regulatory Standards Bill that was introduced in 2011 and again in 2021. Neither progressed at the time. A Regulatory Standards Bill has therefore been rejected by three different Parliaments. The Proposed Bill forms part of the National-Act Coalition Agreement and appears to have majority support. Substance: The Proposed Bill sets out Principles against which new regulatory proposals or existing regulation could be assessed. The Principles would be broad and expressed at a high level, and the Minister for Regulation would be required to produce guidelines that would set out in more detail how the Principles should be interpreted and applied. With some additions, they are based on the 2009 Regulatory Responsibility Taskforceʼs recommended principles as set out in the 2021 Regulatory Standards Bill. New principles focus on the review and maintenance of existing regulation to clarify and strengthen legislative stewardship requirements and require responsible agencies to develop and publicly report against plans to review their stock of legislation. Agencies would be required to ensure that new regulatory proposals are assessed for consistency with relevant principles, and any inconsistencies identified. The Proposed Bill would also enable people to seek independent assessment of whether regulation meets standards through a Regulatory Standards Board to consider consistency with the Principles in response to complaints. The Proposed Bill also gives the Minister for Regulation and the Ministry for Regulation powers to help carry out regulatory review responsibilities, including initiating reviews, setting terms of reference, requiring information, and producing regular performance reports. Improving regulatory efficacy: In EDS’s experience, several factors can undermine regulatory efficacy in Aotearoa New Zealand, including political commitments based on coalition agreements or ideology, inflexible policy development, failure to properly identify problem definitions, and rushed policy deadlines leading to inadequate consultation and deficient Regulatory Impact Statements. The Proposed Bill does not address these issues and cannot be heralded as a solution to regulatory deficiencies. Flawed Principles: The Principles in the Proposed Bill largely mirror previous iterations and are driven by ideology, being contentious, selective and incomplete, inconsistent with international practices, and at risk of creating unintended consequences by prioritising individual liberties over collective interests and the environment while failing to recognise Te Tiriti o Waitangi. Inappropriate powers afforded to the Minister for Regulation: The power vested in the Minister is inappropriate and may lead to unbalanced implementation, including the power to issue guidance on the meaning and application of the Principles, the power to decide which regulations are exempt from compliance, the power to appoint the Board and instruct when it should undertake reviews, and the power to initiate and determine how agency-led regulatory reviews take place. Existing and impending measures addressing regulatory efficacy: Part 4 of the Legislation Act 2019 is set to come into force on 24 March 2026, implementing requirements for lawmakers to release disclosure statements outlining how proposed law complies with legislative guidelines or standards. The Proposed Bill will cut across this process, adding significant burdens and costs. EDS prefers Part 4 of the Legislation Act to be implemented and opposes the Proposed Bill. Recommended changes if the Proposed Bill is to progress: Without derogating from its position that the Proposed Bill should not proceed, EDS recommends including clear guidance on balancing private and public interests, promoting good-faith consultation, prioritising evidence-based decision-making and precautionary approaches, recognising tikanga and Te Tiriti o Waitangi, appointing a Parliamentary Commissioner to manage the recourse mechanism independently, and issuing guidelines jointly by the Attorney-General and the Parliamentary Commissioner. Conclusion: EDS opposes the Proposed Bill as it does not address fundamental issues undermining regulatory efficacy, implements ideological principles, and concentrates excessive power in the hands of the Minister for Regulation. A more independent oversight process and the implementation of existing pending measures like Part 4 of the Legislation Act 2019 are preferred.
